Traditionally it is mostly of hardwood, especially Eucalyptus, taking the trunk or a thick branch, hollowing it out with termites, then removing the bark and trimming the ends, with beeswax possibly added at the mouthpiece end. Modern instruments also use local or imported hardwoods, bamboo, glass, fibreglass, metal, agave, clay, resin, PVC pipe and carbon fibre; the mouthpiece may be shaped, or made of rubber, a drilled rubber stopper or beeswax. The body may be painted or left with the grain showing. The source states no other parts.

The didgeridoo is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 423.121.11, usually cylindrical or conical, between one and three metres long, most about 1.2 metres; longer instruments sound lower, and those with a flared end sound higher. The player produces a sustained bass by vibrating the lips and keeps the sound going with circular breathing. It was developed by the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia and has existed for at least a thousand years; it is now used around the world, but is still most associated with Australian Aboriginal music. Rock paintings show it used in the Ubarr ceremony. Traditionally it is made from hardwood hollowed out by termites, with beeswax possibly added at the mouthpiece.
迪吉里杜管由澳洲北部原住民發展，至少已有一千年歷史；考古研究依岩畫斷代，指出卡卡: The didgeridoo was developed by the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia and is at least a thousand years old; archaeological work, dating the rock paintings, indicates that it has been used in the Kakadu region for less than a thousand years, and that Arnhem Land may be its place of origin. Wilson's 1835 voyage account already draws Aboriginal people of Raffles Bay on Cobourg Peninsula playing it, and bamboo instruments are found in the same area; in 1893 young Etheridge recorded three bamboo trumpets in northern Australia. In 1938 Elkin noted that it was found only in the east Kimberley of Western Australia and the north of the Northern Territory. In the later twentieth century modern designs in non-traditional materials and shapes appeared and provoked argument; today, though used worldwide, it remains most closely associated with Australian Aboriginal music.
迪吉里杜管發出的音色深沉而神秘，帶有原始蒼涼的氣質。其音色暗沉而溫厚，具有濃郁的: The didgeridoo's timbre is deep and mysterious, with a raw, desolate quality. The sound is dark and warm, with a strong hollowness and resonance, and its range is relatively low, mainly in the low and low middle frequencies. The resonance of the wind instrument is distinctive: by circular breathing the player keeps the air inside the tube vibrating continuously, producing a long sustained tone. Its sound lies between a horn and a bassoon, but with a more raw, hoarse texture. Its vibrating energy is strong and readily resonates with the surroundings, and in an open space it carries a long way. Compared with modern wind instruments, the didgeridoo keeps more of the natural, rough character of sound, full of the feel of earth and nature.
